title: Pandya Before Memory Ends
subtitle: Ashoka’s distant whisper, a cave’s thin lines, and the first clear shadow of the fish-bannered south
figure: The early Pandya court and Nedunjeliyan I
era: Early Historic, c. 258 BCE-2nd century BCE
region: Madurai, Korkai and the Tamil south
moral: Fragments can still prove real beginnings.

sources.citation: Ashoka's Major Rock Edicts 2 and 13, c. 258 BCE; D.C. Sircar, Select Inscriptions, Vol. I (1942)
sources.note: Primary Mauryan evidence naming the Pandyas among independent southern peoples.

sources.citation: Mangulam Tamil-Brahmi inscription near Madurai, c. 3rd-2nd century BCE; I. Mahadevan, Early Tamil Epigraphy (Harvard, 2003), R6/R7
sources.note: Earliest datable Pandya ruler-name in Pandya country, tied to Jain cave-bed donations.

sources.citation: Kharavela's Hathigumpha inscription, c. 1st century BCE; K.P. Jayaswal and R.D. Banerji, Epigraphia Indica 20 (1929-30)
sources.note: External evidence for Pandya pearls and a Tamil political confederacy.

panels.shot: sweeping low-angle wide of a hillside cave above scrubland, with Nedunjeliyan standing silhouetted before it under a sky split between dusk and dawn

dialogue.text: Centuries before bards sang of Pandya kings, Ashoka’s rock, a cave wall and a far-off war together whisper the first sure name of Madurai’s fish-bannered south.

panels.shot: epic bird’s-eye of the subcontinent with stylized terrain, from the Himalaya to the southern seas

dialogue.text: In the third century before the Common Era, the Mauryan lion stands over much of the land, but the far south is still a long, dim shape beyond imperial reach.

panels.shot: slow push-in on an Ashokan rock edict carved on a rugged boulder in a dry landscape

dialogue.text: On such rocks, Ashoka orders his words cut into stone. In Major Rock Edicts Two and Thirteen, he names lands he does not rule, but must still address.

panels.shot: tight medium on the inscribed lines with faint superimposed outline of the peninsula’s southern tip in the background

dialogue.text: Among the Cholas, the Cheras, the Satyaputras and Keralaputras, one more name is cut: the Pandyas, independent, coastal, and important enough to be summoned in stone.

panels.shot: documentary-style montage: Ashokan messengers on the road, and imagined Pandya envoys near a southern port

dialogue.text: These edicts speak of dhamma, compassion and restraint even towards distant peoples. By naming the Pandyas, they prove a polity known and recognised, not mere legend at the end of the map.

panels.shot: medium shot of Megasthenes at a Greek-style writing desk, with an imaginative painted map behind him

dialogue.text: Greek writers like Megasthenes will tell of a southern queen called Pandaia, daughter of Heracles. Their stories weave myth, not record; they echo a memory, but cannot guide our steps.

panels.shot: wide shot of early Madurai settlement with wooden palisades, river beyond, and a modest palace complex

dialogue.text: South of the Vaigai, in a growing town that will one day be called Madurai, a Pandya court holds council. The king’s name is not yet on stone, but his power is felt along the fish-rich coast.

panels.shot: intimate interior medium shot of Nedunjeliyan seated in council with a few chiefs, no lavish throne, simple wooden hall

dialogue.text: This early Nedunjeliyan is not yet the hero of later poems. He is a name that will surface beside a cave near Mangulam, tied to men who carve beds for wandering monks.

panels.shot: long shot of Mangulam hill with scrub forest and a small group of workers below

dialogue.text: North of Madurai, near Mangulam, a low hill with natural ledges waits. Here, in the third or second century BCE, hands will cut stone beds beneath the open sky.

panels.shot: close-up of artisans chiselling rock-beds under a rock overhang, with two Jain monks watching quietly

dialogue.text: Early Tamil-Brahmi letters here record donors who prepare these beds for ascetics, likely Jains, seeking shelter from sun and rain as they wander through the Pandya land.

panels.shot: extreme close-up of the Mangulam inscription lines being carved on the rock-bed side

dialogue.text: In one such inscription, later recorded as Mangulam R6 and R7, the donor names are linked by title to a Pandya ruler called Nedunjeliyan, anchoring him in this landscape.

panels.shot: soft focus on the finished inscription with faint silhouettes of a king, officials, and monks layered behind

dialogue.text: The text does not boast of conquests. It traces a web of patronage: officers serving a Nedunjeliyan, making gifts in his time, in his country, to support renouncers under his watch.

panels.shot: medium shot of Nedunjeliyan at dawn visiting the cave with a small entourage, viewing the rock-beds

dialogue.speaker: the_early_pandya_court_and_nedunjeliyan_i
dialogue.text: Let them rest in our land. Their silence harms no one, and steadies men.

panels.shot: low-angle medium close-up of Nedunjeliyan’s face as he listens to a courtier, with faint soundless bustle of Madurai behind

dialogue.text: We do not yet know his campaigns or his court songs. We know only that under his name, officials moved, caves were endowed, and a script took shape on stone.

panels.shot: transition montage: Mangulam inscription fading into Ashokan edict, then into the Hathigumpha inscription on a cliff

dialogue.text: Elsewhere, another king’s record will speak of this south. In the Hathigumpha inscription, the Kalinga ruler Kharavela looks across the sea towards a land of pearls and confederate powers.

panels.shot: wide shot of Kharavela on a balcony overlooking a harbour with ships, imagining distant southern coasts

dialogue.text: Kharavela’s text boasts of reaching the Tamil land and of pearls from the Pandya coast. Across the Bay of Bengal, the wealth of these fisheries has become a line in another king’s self-praise.

panels.shot: evocative wide shot of divers leaping from a boat into clear coastal waters, with heaps of oysters on another boat

dialogue.text: We can see the scene behind the words: divers in the Pandya Gulf, bringing up oysters, merchants weighing pearls, and distant courts measuring the south by what it can send.

panels.shot: medium shot of Nedunjeliyan in a modest court, a trader presenting a small casket, map of coastlines scratched on the floor

dialogue.speaker: the_early_pandya_court_and_nedunjeliyan_i
dialogue.text: Guard the mouths of our rivers. The sea is our field; pearls, our harvest.

panels.shot: reflective shot: a scholar in a modern archive studying estampages of Ashokan, Mangulam, and Hathigumpha inscriptions side by side

dialogue.text: Today, epigraphers like Iravatham Mahadevan read these thin, scattered lines with care, placing scripts in sequence and refusing to stretch them into certainty they cannot bear.

panels.shot: melancholic wide shot of Mangulam hill at sunset, Nedunjeliyan’s translucent figure fading into the rock

dialogue.text: The legend of three great Sangams will be woven much later. Here, in this early age, we have no full court-chronicle—only rock, script and the shadow of a king behind a donor’s name.

panels.shot: low-angle close-up of Nedunjeliyan’s hand touching the rock-bed edge, seamlessly matched to a modern hand tracing the same inscription

dialogue.text: Fragments like Ashoka’s edict, Mangulam’s cave and Hathigumpha’s boast cannot map a Pandya empire, but they prove a real beginning—the first fish carved clearly enough to outlast memory.
